naturalness.evidence: “What were the two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath commanded to do?” is idiomatic English. “Going off duty” naturally describes the end of a shift, and the action options use direct, familiar wording such as “Visit the market” and “Rest at home.”

processing.evidence: Readers must attach “going off duty on the Sabbath” to “the two divisions” and understand those divisions as both receiving the command and performing the requested action. These are ordinary, manageable operations that identify the intended group; they do not introduce substantial avoidable load. The short options are readily compared.

context_economy.evidence: The question supplies no unnecessary setup. “Going off duty on the Sabbath” usefully identifies which divisions are meant, while “commanded to do” directly asks for their assigned action.

structure_assessments.reason: In “the two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath,” the modifier attaches naturally to “divisions,” and the time phrase specifies the duty transition. This information identifies the group without avoidable nesting.

In “were the two divisions … commanded to do,” the passive construction leaves the commander unnamed but makes the divisions’ role clear: they receive the command and carry out the action. Readers need not track an additional participant.
